rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have no baseline for either modality. The central question in a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether combining modalities improves over the best single modality, but this cannot be assessed without knowing how well each modality performs alone. 2) What this tests: config_028 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest possible image-only model—no aggregation, no fusion, a well-understood pretrained encoder. It establishes the performance floor for the image modality and confirms that the pipeline works end-to-end with minimal confounds. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, a clean unimodal baseline is the highest-information first step because (a) it is fast and has few failure modes, (b) it provides the reference needed to interpret every subsequent multimodal result (e.g., config_001, 009, 019), (c) it isolates the image encoder and single-profile setting so that later experiments can cleanly attribute gains to added modalities, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion strategy, and (d) if it already performs strongly, it immediately reshapes the search toward understanding whether RNA adds value rather than wasting budget on multimodal variants that may not help.

1) Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_028: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) yielding ~20.8% accuracy. This establishes a baseline but tells us nothing about whether the RNA modality contributes any signal. 2) Question: config_009 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, weighted) directly tests whether adding an RNA representation (scGPT) to the same image backbone (ResNet50) and same profile setting improves over the image-only baseline. It isolates the multimodal contribution while holding image encoder and profile setting constant. 3) Why best: With only one data point, the highest-uncertainty decision is whether RNA adds value at all. scGPT is a learned biological representation giving RNA its best chance to contribute; weighted fusion is the simplest combination strategy, so a positive result is informative and a negative result is strong. This single experiment tells us whether to invest remaining budget in multimodal exploration or refocus on image-only improvements (encoder choice, multiprofile aggregation).

The two completed experiments show image-only (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak (acc 0.208) while multimodal with scgpt+resnet50 and weighted fusion jumps to 0.421. This large gap tells us RNA information is critical, but it does not decompose how much of the 0.421 comes from the RNA modality alone versus the image modality or their interaction. Config_038 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the cleanest next experiment: it removes the image branch from config_009 while keeping the same RNA encoder and profile setting, isolating the marginal contribution of the image modality. If RNA alone approaches ~0.40, the image adds little and future budget should target RNA encoder or profile improvements; if RNA alone is substantially lower (e.g., ~0.25–0.30), the multimodal fusion is genuinely valuable and we should next optimize fusion strategy and image encoder. Resolving this uncertainty before testing fusion variants (config_012) or image encoder upgrades (config_002) ensures we invest the remaining budget on the modality that actually drives performance, making this the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA (scgpt, singleprofile) is the dominant signal (acc 0.411, F1 0.378), image alone is weak (0.208), and multimodal weighted fusion gives only a marginal gain over RNA alone (0.421 vs 0.411 acc; 0.412 vs 0.378 F1). The profile setting (single vs multi) is a completely unexplored dimension that could substantially shift the performance landscape. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve the RNA representation? This experiment (config_011: rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_038 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt, no aggregation), isolating the multiprofile+aggregation effect on the dominant modality. Why this is best under budget: If multiprofile helps RNA, it justifies investing further experiments in multiprofile multimodal configurations; if it does not, we can confidently restrict the search to singleprofile and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder choice or image encoder quality. Testing this in the RNA-only setting (rather than multimodal) avoids confounding the profile effect with fusion/aggregation interactions, giving the clearest signal about one of the largest unexplored design axes.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) with scgpt boosts RNA-only accuracy from 0.411 (config_038) to 0.530 (config_011), a +0.119 gain. Meanwhile, multimodal singleprofile (config_009, 0.421) barely exceeds RNA singleprofile (0.411), suggesting resnet50 image adds little in the singleprofile regime. The critical open question is whether the multiprofile benefit transfers to the multimodal setting and whether image becomes more useful when RNA is better aggregated. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal, single-variable extension: it adds multiprofile+avgpool to config_009 and adds resnet50+weighted to config_011, keeping all other choices (scgpt, resnet50, weighted) identical to prior runs. This cleanly isolates the interaction between multiprofile aggregation and image fusion, telling us whether to invest further in multimodal multiprofile or focus on RNA-side improvements. Under a tight budget, this one experiment resolves the most important design uncertainty.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_011 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) at 0.530 acc, and the multimodal multiprofile config_019 (same but +resnet50, weighted fusion) only reaches 0.525, suggesting the image adds little with avgpool aggregation. The dominant design question now is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool) can improve the multiprofile representation that drives most of the performance gain. Question: config_032 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_011, isolating the aggregation strategy. Why this is best: If transformer aggregation helps, it identifies a concrete lever to push past 0.530 and informs whether to pair it with multimodal fusion in later experiments. If it does not, we can rule out that direction and focus budget on image encoder quality or fusion strategy. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about an important design axis with one experiment, making it the highest-information next step under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.411 vs image_only 0.208), multiprofile with avgpool is the best setting so far (config_011, scgpt: 0.530), and multimodal with resnet50+weighted does not clearly beat rna_only (config_019: 0.525 ≈ config_011: 0.530). Uncertainty: We have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt) across all experiments. It is unknown whether the learned scgpt representation is essential or whether a simpler linear projection (pca_n2000) captures the same discriminative signal. Question: config_007 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) differs from our best result config_011 only in the RNA encoder, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why best next experiment: RNA is clearly the primary information source, so understanding whether the encoder choice matters is more fundamental than tuning image-side or fusion details. If pca_n2000 matches scgpt, it simplifies the search space and suggests the bottleneck is elsewhere (aggregation, fusion, or image contribution). If scgpt is clearly superior, it confirms we should keep scgpt and focus remaining budget on image encoder or fusion strategy. This is the highest-information single change given current evidence.

The strongest evidence so far is config_007 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, which substantially outperforms scgpt-based multiprofile models (0.514–0.530). The key remaining uncertainty is whether adding the image modality can further improve on this strong RNA signal, or whether it dilutes performance (as seen with scgpt, where multimodal 0.525 ≈ rna_only 0.530). Config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal single-variable extension of config_007: it keeps the same RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation, and only adds the image branch with weighted fusion. This cleanly isolates the contribution of the image modality under the best-performing RNA representation. Under a limited budget, resolving whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile with pca_n2000 is the highest-value question, as it determines whether subsequent experiments should invest in image-encoder upgrades or focus on RNA-side refinements.

Evidence: config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the best result so far at 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1, clearly outperforming the RNA-only baseline (config_007, 0.591) and all scgpt-based configs. The fusion method (weighted vs concat) is the one design axis not yet varied around this best configuration. Question: config_040 changes only the fusion from weighted to concat while holding model_setting, profile_setting, both encoders, and aggregation identical to config_020, giving a clean single-variable test of whether a concatenation-based fusion (letting the classifier learn cross-modal interactions) outperforms a learned weighted sum. Why this is the best next step: under a tight budget, isolating one variable against the current best is the most information-efficient choice. If concat improves on weighted, it identifies a concrete lever to push performance higher; if it does not, we can rule out fusion as a productive direction and redirect budget toward image-encoder or aggregation choices with confidence, rather than spending experiments on a less-informative multi-variable change.

Evidence: The current best is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). We know pca_n2000 >> scgpt for RNA encoding, multiprofile > singleprofile, and weighted > concat fusion. However, the image encoder (resnet50) is the one major design axis not yet explored at the top-performing level—image alone scored only 0.208 with resnet50, suggesting the image branch may be underperforming. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l (config_047) improve over resnet50 while holding all other settings identical to config_020? This is a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the image-encoder effect. Why best next: It directly extends the strongest known configuration along the most impactful untested dimension. If ViT-L helps, we gain a new best and confirm image quality matters; if not, we confirm resnet50 is sufficient and can redirect budget to aggregation or other axes. This is more informative than testing transformer aggregation (where prior scgpt evidence suggests only a ~1.5% gap) or introducing an entirely new RNA encoder (scvi_n200) which would confound multiple variables.
